passages.t: ‘Does the LORD speak only through Moses?’
passages.happening:
“Then Miriam and Aaron criticized Moses because of the Cushite woman he had married, for he had taken a Cushite wife” (verse 1). Then they say what is really on their minds: “Does the LORD speak only through Moses?” they said. “Does He not also speak through us?” (verse 2). “And the LORD heard this.”

The narrator adds a comment: “Now Moses was a very humble man, more so than any man on the face of the earth” (verse 3).

God calls all three to the tent and comes down in the pillar of cloud. To other prophets, he says, he speaks in visions and dreams. “But this is not so with My servant Moses; he is faithful in all My house. I speak with him face to face, clearly and not in riddles; he sees the form of the LORD” (verses 7-8). Then he asks, ‘Why then were you unafraid to speak against My servant Moses?’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
In chapter 11 the challenge to Moses came from the crowd. Now it comes from inside his own family.

Miriam and Aaron are the two best-known leaders after Moses. Miriam is called a prophetess, and she led the women of Israel in song at the sea (Exodus 15:20). Aaron is the high priest. They are also Moses' older sister and brother. In a world where age brought authority, a younger brother raised above them was a real strain.

Their complaint has two parts. The first is about Moses' wife, a Cushite. Cush in the Bible usually means the land south of Egypt along the Nile, in what is now Sudan. On that reading Moses had married a woman from Africa, either after the death of his first wife Zipporah or as a second wife. Others think ‘Cushite’ here means Zipporah herself, since the prophet Habakkuk sets a people called Cushan beside Midian (Habakkuk 3:7), and Zipporah was a Midianite. The text does not settle it.

The second part is the real issue: does God speak only through Moses? Chapter 11 had just shown the Spirit resting on seventy elders. Someone might conclude that Moses was only one voice among many. Miriam and Aaron draw that conclusion in their own favor.

Notice what God does and does not say. He says nothing at all against the marriage. His whole reply is about Moses. Other prophets receive visions and dreams, which need interpreting. With Moses God speaks ‘face to face’. The Hebrew says mouth to mouth. Moses is ‘faithful in all My house’, like a trusted steward who may go into every room.

Verse 3 explains why Moses says nothing in his own defense. The Hebrew word, anav, describes a person who does not grasp at standing. Moses does not defend himself, and God defends him. Many readers, both traditional and critical, take the verse as a comment by someone other than Moses, since a humble man would hardly write it of himself.

In the Hebrew of verse 1 the verb ‘criticized’ is feminine and singular. That suggests Miriam took the lead.
passages.later:
The prophet Micah names all three as God's gift to Israel: “I sent Moses before you, as well as Aaron and Miriam” (Micah 6:4).

Hebrews builds on God's words about Moses to say who Jesus is: “Now Moses was faithful as a servant in all God’s house, testifying to what would be spoken later. But Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house” (Hebrews 3:5-6).

John's Gospel goes beyond even the nearness Moses had: “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18).
passages.hard:
Was the complaint about Moses' wife a matter of race? And does this chapter say anything about skin color?

The text does not say what troubled Miriam about the marriage. Some readers think her objection was to a foreign wife, who may well have been a dark-skinned African woman. Others think the marriage was an excuse, and that the real grievance was the one in verse 2, rivalry over who speaks for God.

On either reading one thing is plain. God does not criticize the marriage. He does not criticize the woman. His anger falls on the two who spoke against Moses. If the objection was to a Cushite wife because she was a Cushite, the chapter gives that objection no support at all. It rebukes the people who made it.

The Bible has been misused to rank human beings by the color of their skin and to forbid marriages between people of different peoples. This chapter cannot be made to say that. The only marriage to a woman from Africa that it mentions is Moses' own, and God defends the man who made it. Every person of every people is made in the image of God.
passages.asks: Miriam and Aaron asked whether God did not speak through them too. Ask where you resent the place God has given to someone else, perhaps someone younger than you or close to you. And ask how you respond when you are criticized: by defending yourself at once, or by leaving room for God to do it.

passages.t: Miriam outside the camp, and Israel waiting
passages.happening:
When the cloud lifts, “suddenly Miriam became leprous, white as snow” (verse 10). Aaron turns to Moses: “My lord, please do not hold against us this sin we have so foolishly committed” (verse 11).

“So Moses cried out to the LORD, ‘O God, please heal her!’” (verse 13).

God answers that she must be shut outside the camp for seven days, and then she may be brought back (verse 14). “So Miriam was confined outside the camp for seven days, and the people did not move on until she was brought in again” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The disease is the one Leviticus 13 describes, a condition of the skin that older Bibles called leprosy. It was not the illness known by that name today. The marks of it, pale and flaking skin, looked like death, and Aaron says so in his plea (verse 12).

The story turns round on itself. The sister and brother who asked whether God speaks through them now need Moses to speak to God for them. Aaron, the elder, calls his younger brother ‘My lord’.

Moses' prayer is five words in Hebrew, one of the shortest in the Bible. The man they had spoken against prays for the one who spoke. He does not wait for an apology from her. He does not make a speech. He asks God to heal her.

God's answer draws on the customs of honor and shame. If a father had publicly shamed his daughter, she would have borne the disgrace for seven days. Seven days was also the period the law set for shutting a person apart to see whether a skin condition would pass (Leviticus 13:4-5). The words ‘after that she may be brought back in’ show that she is healed and restored. The seven days are a limit. Her exclusion has an end, fixed in advance.

Then comes a detail that is easy to pass over. The whole camp, with its tribes and its cloud and its trumpets, does not move for a week. Israel does not leave Miriam behind. The nation waits for one woman.

Why was Miriam struck and not Aaron? The text does not say. Some point to the feminine verb in verse 1 as a sign that she led. Others suggest that the high priest could not be made unclean without halting Israel's worship, or that watching his sister struck and pleading for her was Aaron's own humbling. The chapter keeps its attention on the healing Moses asked for and God gave.
passages.later:
The law later pointed back to this day as a warning to take skin disease seriously: ‘Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam’ (Deuteronomy 24:9).

Jesus taught his followers to do what Moses did here: “But I tell you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).
passages.hard:
Does this story mean that skin disease, or any illness, is a punishment from God? And is there a meaning in the words ‘white as snow’?

No to the first. This is the story of one person at one moment, told as a sign that confirmed God's word about Moses. It is not a rule about illness. The law of Leviticus 13 makes no link between this disease and a person's sin, and Jesus refused to treat suffering as proof of wrongdoing: “Neither this man nor his parents sinned” (John 9:3). No one may point to Miriam and tell a sick person that they are being punished.

On the second, ‘white as snow’ describes diseased skin. The same phrase is used of Moses' own hand in Exodus 4:6 and of Gehazi in 2 Kings 5:27. It is a picture of sickness and of something like death. It is not a statement about the worth of any shade of healthy skin, light or dark, and it has nothing to do with race. Some readers have noticed an irony, if Miriam had objected to a dark-skinned wife and was then struck with skin gone white. If that irony is intended, it falls on the one who despised another person. Any use of this chapter to say that one color of skin is better or worse than another is a misuse of Scripture, and it is wrong.

It needs to be said plainly. The Bible does not teach that sickness comes from too little faith, or that a person who stays ill did not believe enough. Paul prayed and was not healed, and no one blames him. If you live with chronic illness, pain or disability, you are not a failure of faith. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Moses' whole prayer for the sister who had wronged him was five words, and the camp waited a week for her to come home. Ask whom you could pray for today in one honest sentence, though they have spoken against you. And ask who has been left outside in your church or family, and whether anyone is waiting for them.
